title: Hex Digits of a 32-Bit Integer
statement:
You get a 32-bit signed integer num. Return it written in base 16, using the digits 0–9 and the lowercase letters a–f, with no leading zeros. Zero is written "0".

A negative number is written as its 32-bit two's complement bit pattern, the same 8 hex digits a CSS colour picker or a memory dump would show for those 32 bits. So -1 becomes "ffffffff".

Do not use a built-in base conversion such as toString(16) or hex(); produce the digits yourself.

examples.why: 4011 = 15·256 + 10·16 + 11, so the digits are f, a, b.
In 32 bits, −2 is all ones except the last bit. A minus sign is never written.
The two zero digits at the end are real digits and stay; only leading zeros are dropped.

hints: One hex digit stands for exactly four bits. How do you read the lowest four bits of a number?
num & 15 gives the last hex digit. Then shift the number right by four bits and repeat.
For negatives, use an unsigned (zero-filling) shift so the loop stops after at most 8 digits, or first map the value into 0..2³² − 1.

explain.intuition:
Base 16 lines up perfectly with binary: every hex digit is one group of four bits. So you do not need division at all. Mask off the lowest four bits (num & 15), look up that digit, and shift the number four bits to the right. Repeat until nothing is left.

Negatives are where people trip. In JavaScript, >> copies the sign bit in from the left, so a negative number never reaches zero. Use >>>, which fills with zeros. In Python, integers have no fixed width, so first take num & 0xffffffff to get the 32-bit pattern as a non-negative number.
steps: Turn the value into its unsigned 32-bit pattern (num >>> 0 in JS, num & 0xffffffff in Python).
While the value is not 0: push "0123456789abcdef"[value & 15], then shift the value right by 4 bits.
The digits came out lowest first, so reverse them and join.
pitfalls: Using an arithmetic shift (>>) on a negative number. The sign bit keeps refilling and the loop never ends.
Returning an empty string for 0, because the loop body never runs.
Writing negatives with a minus sign, like "-2", instead of the two's complement digits.

solutions.title: Divide by 16 after making it unsigned
solutions.idea: Add 2³² to a negative number to get its unsigned value, then take remainders by 16 like any base conversion.

solutions.title: Mask four bits, shift four bits
solutions.idea: Each hex digit is one nibble. Read the lowest nibble with & 15 and drop it with an unsigned shift.

followups: Convert a hex string back to a signed 32-bit integer.
Generalise to any base that is a power of two, such as octal or base 32.
